    • Recent findings suggest that few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee.
    • Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee. Merchants resent the cut that card-issuing banks and payment networks take from every sale, and consumers resent checkout fees for paying by credit card.Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves. The first to act, Illinois, reads federal banking law in a way that lets an out-of-state bank escape its rules only by opening a physical branch there. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has rightly proposed a rule to end that absurdity.Illinois’ Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, set to take effect in July 2027, bars banks from collecting swipe fees on the sales tax and tip portion of a purchase. But federal law exempts national banks from this kind of state regulation, and Congress extended this protection to state-chartered banks to create parity.Illinois reads that protection as covering only those with a physical branch in the state. A small bank in Iowa serving Illinois customers from across the line may have to comply; an identical institution with an Illinois branch is exempt.>>> The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall StreetThat’s wrong, and the FDIC is right to try to fix it.States have a legitimate, long-standing role in protecting consumers and regulating commerce within their borders. But the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states, and for good reason. Without a strong defense of Commerce Clause principles, a few states can bully the rest into following their rules. For multi-state banks, Congress has already set a reasonable standard.Anyone who has worked on state policy, as I did in Arizona, knows the governing principle: in-state presence. An out-of-state business with a substantial in-state presence—such as a physical location—answers to that state’s rules.When the Supreme Court’s 2018 Wayfair decision let states require remote sellers to collect sales tax, the fight was over whether less than a physical presence could count. Nobody ever suggested opening a store in Arizona would exempt a seller from its sales tax.Illinois’ reading of federal banking law produces exactly that absurd result. The provision at issue, from the Riegle-Neal Act, refers to out-of-state banks’ “branches” in the host state, and Illinois reads that word as a limit. Approve a card purchase for a customer passing through Illinois, with no physical location there, and Illinois may say you are subject to its law. Open a branch, and suddenly you are exempt.The result is a regulatory reach that shrinks as a bank’s presence grows. The few state banks based outside Illinois but with a branch there would be exempt, while the 3,185 state banks the FDIC identifies as potentially affected (most of them small) would not. Those banks could spend the resources to comply, but to get an exemption, they would perversely have to open a branch there.That’s not what Congress set out to do. Riegle-Neal was a law about interstate banking and branching, written when banks served customers through branches and the first iPhone was more than a decade away. When Congress amended it in 1997, the bill’s sponsor was plain about the goal: “The essence of this legislation is to provide parity between state-chartered banks and national banks.”Turning a word that described 1990s banking into a penalty on modern remote service banking gets that purpose backward and destroys parity.>>> The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the SameThe FDIC’s proposal applies the sensible reading. Where a host state’s law does not apply to an out-of-state national bank, it does not apply to an out-of-state state bank either, branch or no branch. The rule does not replace state regulation with federal regulation; it restores common sense and legislative intent to a 1990s-era statute.If anything, Illinois’ reading works against state authority. The dual banking system, which lets a bank choose a state or federal charter, is itself an expression of federalism. Make the state charter the costlier one, and, as the FDIC observes, banks could shift to federal charters. That would be a strange victory indeed for states’ rights.It also would be an expensive one. The FDIC estimates the affected state banks would spend about $308 million up front and nearly $7 million a year complying, all to transfer roughly $2.3 million a year in fees from banks to merchants. With 11 other states having explored similar legislation, the problem is unlikely to stay in Illinois.If federal law has gone too far or failed to account for state needs in a card-dependent, network-based economy, it’s Congress’ job to amend it. But no reasonable reading of that framework would exempt a bank for moving into a state while penalizing its competitor for staying home.The FDIC has proposed saying that clearly. It should finalize the rule. A bank shouldn’t have to move into Illinois to get out from under Illinois law.

    Recent findings suggest that few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee. Merchants resent the cut that card-issuing banks and payment networks take from every sale, and consumers resent checkout fees for paying by credit card.

    Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves. The first to act, Illinois, reads federal banking law in a way that lets an out-of-state bank escape its rules only by opening a physical branch there. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has rightly proposed a rule to end that absurdity.

    Recent findings suggest that illinois’ Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, set to take effect in July 2027, bars banks from collecting swipe fees on the sales tax and tip portion of a purchase. But federal law exempts national banks from this kind of state regulation, and Congress extended this protection to state-chartered banks to create parity.

    Illinois reads that protection as covering only those with a physical branch in the state. A small bank in Iowa serving Illinois customers from across the line may have to comply; an identical institution with an Illinois branch is exempt.

    >>> The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall Street.

    That’s wrong, and the FDIC is right to try to fix it.

    States have a legitimate, long-standing role in protecting consumers and regulating commerce within their borders. But the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states, and for good reason. Without a strong defense of Commerce Clause principles, a few states can bully the rest into following their rules. For multi-state banks, Congress has already set a reasonable standard.

    Anyone who has worked on state policy, as I did in Arizona, knows the governing principle: in-state presence. An out-of-state business with a substantial in-state presence—such as a physical location—answers to that state’s rules.

    Sources indicate that when the Supreme Court’s 2018 Wayfair decision let states require remote sellers to collect sales tax, the fight was over whether less than a physical presence could count. Nobody ever suggested opening a store in Arizona would exempt a seller from its sales tax.

    According to recent reports, illinois’ reading of federal banking law produces exactly that absurd result. The provision at issue, from the Riegle-Neal Act, refers to out-of-state banks’ “branches” in the host state, and Illinois reads that word as a limit. Approve a card purchase for a customer passing through Illinois, with no physical location there, and Illinois may say you are subject to its law. Open a branch, and suddenly you are exempt.

    The result is a regulatory reach that shrinks as a bank’s presence grows. The few state banks based outside Illinois but with a branch there would be exempt, while the 3,185 state banks the FDIC identifies as potentially affected (most of them small) would not. Those banks could spend the resources to comply, but to get an exemption, they would perversely have to open a branch there.

    Industry observers note that that’s not what Congress set out to do. Riegle-Neal was a law about interstate banking and branching, written when banks served customers through branches and the first iPhone was more than a decade away. When Congress amended it in 1997, the bill’s sponsor was plain about the goal: “The essence of this legislation is to provide parity between state-chartered banks and national banks.”.

    Turning a word that described 1990s banking into a penalty on modern remote service banking gets that purpose backward and destroys parity.

    >>> The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the Same.

    The FDIC’s proposal applies the sensible reading. Where a host state’s law does not apply to an out-of-state national bank, it does not apply to an out-of-state state bank either, branch or no branch. The rule does not replace state regulation with federal regulation; it restores common sense and legislative intent to a 1990s-era statute.

    Industry observers note that if anything, Illinois’ reading works against state authority. The dual banking system, which lets a bank choose a state or federal charter, is itself an expression of federalism. Make the state charter the costlier one, and, as the FDIC observes, banks could shift to federal charters. That would be a strange victory indeed for states’ rights.

    It also would be an expensive one. The FDIC estimates the affected state banks would spend about $308 million up front and nearly $7 million a year complying, all to transfer roughly $2.3 million a year in fees from banks to merchants. With 11 other states having explored similar legislation, the problem is unlikely to stay in Illinois.

    If federal law has gone too far or failed to account for state needs in a card-dependent, network-based economy, it’s Congress’ job to amend it. But no reasonable reading of that framework would exempt a bank for moving into a state while penalizing its competitor for staying home.

    The FDIC has proposed saying that clearly. It should finalize the rule. A bank shouldn’t have to move into Illinois to get out from under Illinois law.

    It has been revealed that not long ago, I drifted through a handful of old European cities. What stayed with me was neither the cathedrals nor the cafés with their thimbles of ferocious coffee.

    It was the organization the bronze kept: The squares belonged to poets and playwrights, astronomers and philosophers, figures in stone cloaks gazing over bustling pigeons as if weighing one more line. Here and there, a statesman sulked on his plinth, and the courthouses guarded their jurists, but officeholders were scarce.

    The exception was the kings, those equestrian gentlemen forever reining in horses that never move.

    Industry observers note that the pattern has a plausible explanation. Europe was hardly a stranger to electoral politics. Athenian citizens voted in assembly, the Roman Republic chose its consuls, Iceland’s Althing has convened since 930, and Venice elected its doges for roughly 11 centuries.

    Sources indicate that so, the scarcity of political monuments cannot be explained by the absence of voting. A better account is that a reputation lasts about as long as the work behind it remains usable.

    >>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State.

    According to recent reports, A literary or scientific achievement keeps functioning. Dante’s “Commedia,” Shakespeare’s plays, and Newton’s “Principia” can still be met directly, without an intermediary, and they answer questions each generation asks anew.

    A statesman’s achievement, by contrast, is tied to the circumstance that called it forth: a treaty, a succession crisis, a levy. Once that circumstance passes, the achievement survives chiefly as historical record. The principal lessons learned from political figures are the consequences of their decisions rather than the reasoning that produced them, which is seldom preserved and less often consulted.

    Political monuments are also unusually exposed to revision. The removal of Lenin statues across the former Eastern Bloc after 1989, and the toppling of Edward Colston in Bristol in 2020, suggest that a statesman’s standing stays open to dispute in a way a poet’s rarely does. Southerners know this quite well, having watched Confederate monuments come down in town after town.

    Which brings me home to Auburn, where the statuary has another temperament altogether. Ours wear shoulder pads. Heisman winners stride eternally outside Jordan-Hare, and Shug Jordan keeps his vigil.

    Sources indicate that I love a Saturday on the Plains as dearly as anyone alive. But an athlete’s fame is the briefest bloom in the garden, briefer even than a senator’s. Who toasts the champions of antiquity? The wrestlers and charioteers of Olympia survive mostly because Pindar wrote odes to them. They endure, in other words, by the grace of a poet.

    So it was with a small, private gladness that I read the news: Auburn confirmed a $22 million investment from the state of Alabama, “championed by Gov. Kay Ivey, an Auburn alumna, to establish the Kay Ivey Institute for Civic Leadership.” At last, we may raise a monument to the kind of figure the Old World remembers.

    Auburn enters a crowded and quickening field. Recently, I mentioned the civics centers popping up across many institutions and states. Ohio has committed $24 million to create civic-education centers at five public universities. The ones to beat are well known: Florida, with its Hamilton School for Classical and Civic Education; Texas, with its School of Civic Leadership and Civitas Institute; and Tennessee, whose Institute of American Civics was established in 2022 by the state’s general assembly.

    These programs now count in the standings too, since City Journal’s newly introduced college-ranking system rewards institutions that host a School of Civic Thought. It’s high time, isn’t it, that Auburn’s name sat atop that list?

    According to recent reports, of our own institute, we know very little. The university notes its academic direction, programming and long-term priorities will be developed in the coming months, so my hopes go out wearing a raincoat.

    >>> A Columbus Day Question—Have We Finally Stopped Distorting Our Past?

    Recent findings suggest that still, the opportunity is plain. Auburn could gather some of the most distinguished and exacting scholars in the humanities: historians, political theorists, legal minds, and philosophers. Those disciplines are the timbers from which civic life is built.

    It has been revealed that the town’s growing. It’s a fine place to live and think, and its research already commands respect well beyond the state line.

    In a recent development, the old oaks at Toomer’s Corner stood since the late 1930s. They died because of football. After Auburn beat Alabama in 2010, an aggrieved rival poured herbicide into their roots.

    Industry observers note that their replacements fared little better. One was set ablaze during a celebration after a win over Louisiana State University, and the corner has been replanted more than once since.

    It has been revealed that passion for a game can kill the very things it gathers around. Yet something survived. Saplings grown from the original oaks’ acorns now line the walk from the corner to Samford Hall. The descendants of those trees mark a path from the place where we celebrate to the place where we study.

    If the Ivey Institute is built with care, more of us may follow that path. Someday, a visitor may find, among the halfbacks, a philosopher in bronze. Better still, he may find generations of graduates who read the founders as eagerly as they read a box score.

    That would be a monument no poison or match could take down.

    The economy exceeded analysts’ expectations in October. Friday’s monthly employment report not only indicates an additional 165,000 jobs, but also revises upward the previous two months. Including those revisions, the total increase is just under a quarter million jobs. And the internals of the report are even better.

    Recent findings suggest that the number of jobs in the report comes from a survey of businesses, but there’s also a survey of households that produces employment and unemployment estimates. This survey showed that 463,000 more Americans were employed in October than September, and 1.4 million more than July, pushing down the unemployment rate.

    Recent findings suggest that people are entering the labor market in droves, and they’re able to find jobs. That’s why labor force participation has reversed its multi-year slide and is up for three consecutive months, same as the employment-to-population ratio. Americans are not only looking for jobs but finding them.

    Sources indicate that there’s even good news on the types of jobs being created. All net job growth last month came from full-time work, while part-time jobs actually declined as people moved from part-time to full-time work. Additionally, the number of people with multiple jobs declined, signally many folks exchanged multiple part-time jobs for a single full-time one. Another sign of labor market strength.

    >>> Americans, Job Market Need Workforce Pell Grants.

    Since July, full-time jobs are now up a whopping 1.5 million while part-time jobs have declined, so all net job growth over the last three months has been full-time work, which tends to have better pay and benefits compared to part-time.

    There’s more good news regarding where all these jobs are being created. More than 96 percent of October’s job growth came from the productive private sector. The government added only 6,000 jobs, all of which came from state governments while the federal bureaucracy added no jobs at all.

    Within the private sector, most areas of the economy added jobs in October, including manufacturing. This sector in particular is noteworthy because payrolls were declining for three years as the sector hemorrhaged jobs from 2023 through 2025. That downward trend was finally reversed this year, and now manufacturing jobs are at their highest level since December 2024.

    Sources indicate that so, despite all the fearmongering of AI taking everyone’s job, employers went on a hiring spree last month and Americans are pouring into the labor market. This dynamic was especially true of college graduates, a group that was supposed to be directly in the crosshairs of AI, but whose employment level shot up by 422,000 in October.

    According to recent reports, that means the number of college grads working today is more than 2 million higher than in July. To be clear, AI is certainly eliminating some jobs, and that will continue as the technology evolves and is adopted. But it’s also creating even more opportunities for work, just like any disruptive technology, from the steam locomotive to the internet.

    >>> Why Aren’t Employers Hiring Right Now?

    It should be no surprise that when student loan repayment restarted, millions of college grads decided to look for work again. Having a bill to pay—instead of foisting that debt on the backs of taxpayers—is a powerful motivator to find work, even if you have a gender studies degree.

    Ending the student loan repayment “pauses” that began six years ago is just one example of how current public policy is promoting a strong labor market. Throw in tax cuts like full expensing for businesses along with massive reductions in burdensome regulations and you have a great landscape to increase economic growth and employment.

    It has been revealed that tax and regulatory reform are principally responsible for the economy being on track to increase private fixed investment by 10 percent or more this year. That category of investment is extremely important because it’s the driver of long-run economic growth. It’s where we get everything from factories to software—all the things that increase productivity and wage growth.

    That increased wage growth is already here, but it’s been swallowed by higher energy prices ever since February due to the Iran war. Although the average American’s weekly paycheck bought less in October than it did in February, it’s at least estimated to have bought slightly more than in September.

    It has been revealed that the fallout from the Iran war is the only fly in the ointment from the October jobs report. Were it not for higher prices, workers would grade this economy an “A plus.”.

    It has been revealed that A Upcoming York attorney was sentenced Thursday to eight months in prison for embezzling over $500,000 from a trust that he oversaw, according to the Connecticut U.S. attorney’s office.

    Recent findings suggest that edward W. Miller, 71, of Lawrence, New York, was sentenced to prison by U.S. District Judge Sarala V. Nagala in Hartford, Connecticut.

    David X. Sullivan, the U.S. attorney for the District of Connecticut, confirmed the sentence after Miller was found guilty of stealing more than $500,000 from a property trust that he managed from February 2016 to September 2022, owned by a person identified as “M.P.” in court records.

    Miller used his position as a trustee to write and negotiate unauthorized checks that he then made payable to himself, his law practice and family members, according to prosecutors and coverage by Law360.

    It has been revealed that miller pleaded guilty to wire fraud earlier this year and said he refinanced his home to pay back the trust. Miller made full restitution of $509,372.82, part of a settlement of a separate civil lawsuit filed by the victims.

    In addition to eight months in prison, Miller was also sentenced to one year of supervised release.

    Breaking: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, today, in Texas v.
    • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
    • During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

    The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

    During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

    The State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

    The district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

    We conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

    The enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

    In a recent development, through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

    Recent findings suggest that judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

    In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and new parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

    According to recent reports, on May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

    1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

    According to recent reports, H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

    It has been revealed that section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

    At concern here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

    Even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

    After the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

    Industry observers note that the $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

    In a recent development, texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

    In a recent development, I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a fresh requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

    Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

    Sources indicate that judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

    Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

    Sources indicate that I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

    Industry observers note that the petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the new Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

    More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

    Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

    According to recent reports, after a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

    Market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

    Democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to new data centers had been building.

    According to recent reports, investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

    >>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

    Sources indicate that the fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

    The fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

    Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer fresh commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

    Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

    Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

    >>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

    Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

    So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

    It has been revealed that the administration retains broad authority to concern executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

    Democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

    According to recent reports, the president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or fresh regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

    Sources indicate that the economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

    The U.S. Navy Needs a Upcoming Battlecruiser. Will It Get One?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding plan called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a upcoming, modern class of battleship.

    • By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding plan called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a upcoming, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” WarshipThe unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.>>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile launches, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.>>> To Build the Golden FleetHow the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol HillWhile battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.Resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    Industry observers note that last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding plan called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a new, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

    By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

    The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

    In a recent development, the unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

    Industry observers note that >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

    It has been revealed that the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

    In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

    In a recent development, the combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

    Recent findings suggest that the damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile rolls out, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

    >>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

    How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that while battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

    Sources indicate that keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the upcoming AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

    Industry observers note that in time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

    Resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious blueprint, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

    This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Heritage ↗ Open Full Page

    Rule 14a-8: Perhaps Slow-Walking Recission is Best

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission.
    • In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission.
    • To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the concern, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having said that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.For example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation ProposalsTo illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a firm would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.Third, sustainability commitments are said to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.>>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESGAll the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too promptly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.Much more can, should, and will be said about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”.

    In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the issue, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.

    To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having remarked that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.

    Sources indicate that for example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.

    The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.

    In a recent development, while our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”.

    >>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation Proposals.

    Recent findings suggest that to illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a company would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.

    Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.

    Recent findings suggest that third, sustainability commitments are stated to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.

    Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.

    In a recent development, if these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.

    >>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESG.

    All the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.

    Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.

    All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too quickly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.

    Much more can, should, and will be mentioned about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”.
